claims.text: The hypothesis applies to as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi thin films and lithographically patterned nanoribbons.
Rapid deposition and patterning produce a high defect density and internal stress in these films and nanoribbons.
Nanoscale structural inhomogeneities and internal stress fields are the predominant factors governing the magnetocaloric response and hysteresis.
Internal stress and defects pin magnetic domains in the as-deposited material.
Structural inhomogeneity and distributed magnetic-domain switching broaden the temperature range of the magnetocaloric entropy-change feature.
Stress-induced domain pinning increases hysteresis and energy dissipation during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
A low-to-moderate-temperature post-deposition anneal will partially relieve internal stress.
The anneal can relieve stress without significantly changing composition or the overall microstructure.
Annealing will reduce defect-induced domain-wall pinning and homogenize the magnetic-domain structure.
Reduced pinning after annealing will enable more coherent spin realignment during field cycling.
Annealing will produce a sharper entropy-change peak with a narrower temperature range than the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing will increase the maximum entropy change relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing will reduce magnetic hysteresis losses relative to the as-deposited baseline.
The shape and temperature width of the entropy-change curve and hysteretic losses are relevant observables for evaluating magnetocaloric refrigeration performance.
The proposed stress-pinning mechanism will dominate in nanoscale or patterned non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi under low applied fields.
Heat-transfer rate is the limiting factor for magnetic-cooling cycle frequency within the stated operating boundary.

Failure of annealed samples to show statistically significant peak sharpening, increased maximum entropy change, and reduced hysteresis relative to unannealed controls would falsify the proposed mechanism.
